current: Then, tending his father-in-law's flock near Mount Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning without being consumed — and from it God calls his name twice, revealing the divine name YHWH for the first time, and charging Moses with the impossible task: go to Pharaoh and bring my people out of Egypt.
problem: The name YHWH is used throughout Genesis, including by God to Abraham and Jacob. At the bush God explains the name (Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh) and tells Moses to use it; Exodus 6:3 says the patriarchs did not 'know' God by it, which commentators read as not experiencing what it means, not as a first mention.
evidence: Genesis 15:7 'I am GOD [YHWH] who brought you out from Ur'; Genesis 28:13 'I am the ETERNAL, the God of your father Abraham'; Exodus 3:14-15 'Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh... GOD [יהוה], the God of your fathers... This shall be My name forever' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Genesis.15.7, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.3.14-15)
fix: Then, tending his father-in-law's flock near Mount Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning without being consumed. From it God calls his name twice, tells Moses the divine name and its meaning ('I will be what I will be'), and gives him the impossible task: go to Pharaoh and bring my people out of Egypt.

current: Moses's birth story has an exact parallel in the Legend of Sargon of Akkad (c. 2300 BCE), in which the great Mesopotamian king describes being born secretly, placed in a reed basket waterproofed with bitumen, and set on a river where he was found and raised by a royal gardener — a 'hidden origins' narrative pattern also known in other ancient hero stories.
problem: Not an 'exact' parallel (in Sargon's legend his own mother abandons him and a water-drawer raises him; no royal adoption). The finder was Akki, a drawer of water, who made Sargon his gardener, not a royal gardener. c. 2300 BCE is when Sargon lived; the legend text is a Neo-Assyrian composition of the 7th century BCE.
evidence: Wikipedia, Sargon of Akkad, Birth legend: 'Akki, the drawer of water... took me as his son and reared me', 'appointed me as his gardener', basket sealed 'with bitumen'; the Neo-Assyrian text dates to 'the 7th century BC' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargon_of_Akkad)
fix: Moses's birth story is similar to the Legend of Sargon of Akkad, a text known from 7th-century BCE Assyrian copies, in which the king says his mother bore him in secret, put him in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and set it on the river, where Akki, a water-drawer, found him and raised him as his gardener.

current: The store cities of Pithom and Pi-Ramesses (Raamses) mentioned as Israelite labor projects are archaeologically real: Pi-Ramesses was the spectacular capital built by Ramesses II (r. 1279–1213 BCE) in the eastern Nile Delta, and excavations have uncovered its enormous scale.
problem: Pi-Ramesses is well excavated, but Pithom's location is disputed (Tell el-Retaba vs Tell el-Maskhuta), and matching the Bible's Pithom and Raamses to these sites is a scholarly identification, not an archaeological certainty.
evidence: Wikipedia, Pithom: 'Some scholars identified it as... Tell el-Maskhuta... Others identified it as the earlier archaeological site of Tell El Retabeh'; Maskhuta had 'a long break until the late 7th century BC' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pithom)
fix: Raamses is usually identified with Pi-Ramesses, the capital built by Ramesses II (r. 1279–1213 BCE) in the eastern Nile Delta, whose enormous scale excavations have revealed; Pithom's location is still debated between two Delta sites, Tell el-Retaba and Tell el-Maskhuta.

current: The practice of using conquered or enslaved Semitic labor for monumental building projects is well-documented in Egyptian records, including the Leiden Papyrus which describes rations distributed to 'Apiru laborers making bricks' — a word some scholars connect to 'Hebrew.'
problem: Papyrus Leiden 348 orders grain for 'Apiru who are hauling stone for a great pylon, not making bricks, and the quoted phrase is not in the text. Most scholars now see the 'Apiru-Hebrew link as indirect at best.
evidence: Sources and parallels of the Exodus (Wikipedia): 'Issue grain to the men of the army and (to) the ʿApiru who are drawing stone for the great pylon of the [...] of Ramesses' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sources_and_parallels_of_the_Exodus); Wikipedia ʿApiru: 'most contemporary scholars now regard the connection as indirect' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habiru)
fix: Egyptian records do mention foreign laborers on royal building projects: Papyrus Leiden 348, from the reign of Ramesses II, orders grain for 'the 'Apiru who are drawing stone for the great pylon' of a Ramesses building. Early scholars linked the word 'Apiru to 'Hebrew,' but most now see the connection as indirect.

current: Moses is the most important human figure in the Torah, yet the rabbis were careful to keep him human: the Passover Haggadah, recited at every seder, mentions Moses's name only once — to prevent the exodus story from becoming the story of Moses rather than the story of God.
problem: That Moses appears once in the Haggadah (in the quoted verse Exodus 14:31) is correct, but the purpose is a later explanation, not a stated rabbinic decision; it is presented as documented intent.
evidence: Gateways, 'Where is Moshe?': Moses appears once, in the verse 'the nation believed in G-d and in Moses His servant', and 'one explanation is that the Haggadah is not the story of Moses but the story of everyone' (https://www.gatewaysonline.org/where-is-moshe/)
fix: Moses is the most important human figure in the Torah, yet the Passover Haggadah names him only once, inside a quoted verse; a common explanation is that the seder tells the story of God freeing the whole people, not the story of Moses.

current: God calling Moses's name twice ('Moses! Moses!') is one of four times in the Torah God calls a name twice, each marking a moment of supreme urgency and intimacy.
problem: The midrash lists Abraham, Jacob and Moses in the Torah and Samuel in the book of Samuel: three in the Torah, four in the whole Bible.
evidence: Shemot Rabbah 2:6: 'You find in "Abraham, Abraham" (Genesis 22:11)... "Jacob, Jacob" (Genesis 46:2)... "Samuel, Samuel" (I Samuel 3:10)... However, "Moses Moses," there is no pasek between them' and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: 'an expression of fondness and encouragement' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Shemot_Rabbah.2.6)
fix: God calling Moses's name twice ('Moses! Moses!') is one of three such double calls in the Torah, with Abraham and Jacob (a fourth, Samuel, is in the Prophets); the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 2:6) reads the doubling as an expression of fondness and encouragement.

current: Yocheved; Miriam
problem: Neither is named in this parsha: Exodus 2 calls them 'a woman of Levi' and 'his sister'. Jochebed is first named in Exodus 6:20 (Vaera), Miriam in 15:20 (Beshalach). The identification is correct but it comes from those later verses.
evidence: Exodus 2:1-2 'a woman of Levi... bore a son'; 2:4 'his sister stationed herself at a distance'; 6:20 'Amram took to wife... Jochebed, and she bore him Aaron and Moses'; 15:20 'Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.2.1-4)
fix: Replace with "Moses's mother (Yocheved)" and "Moses's sister (Miriam)".

current: When Pharaoh refuses to let the Israelites go, God unleashes the first seven plagues upon Egypt: water turning to blood, frogs, lice, wild animals, livestock disease, boils, and devastating hail — each time Pharaoh hardens his heart and refuses.
problem: After the boils the Torah says God hardened Pharaoh's heart, not Pharaoh himself; the summary erases the distinction that the jewishTradition field then discusses.
evidence: Exodus 9:12 'But GOD stiffened the heart of Pharaoh, and he would not heed them' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.9.12)
fix: When Pharaoh refuses to let the Israelites go, God brings the first seven plagues upon Egypt: water turning to blood, frogs, lice, wild animals, livestock disease, boils, and devastating hail. Each time Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he refuses.

current: When he and Aaron first appear before Pharaoh, the court magicians match Aaron's staff-into-serpent trick (though Aaron's serpent swallows theirs), and Pharaoh dismisses them.
problem: Moses and Aaron first went to Pharaoh in Exodus 5:1 (in Shemot); the staff-into-serpent scene in 7:10 is their second audience.
evidence: Exodus 5:1 'Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "...Let My people go"'; Exodus 7:10 'So Moses and Aaron came before Pharaoh... Aaron cast down his rod' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.5.1, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.7.10)
fix: When he and Aaron return to Pharaoh, the court magicians match Aaron's staff-into-serpent sign (though Aaron's serpent swallows theirs), and Pharaoh dismisses them.

current: Then the plagues begin in earnest, structured in a deliberate 3-3-1 pattern: the first plague of each triad is announced at the Nile, the second at the palace, the third without warning.
problem: The pattern commentators describe is three sets of three (plus the tenth plague), not 3-3-1; this parsha simply stops after the first plague of the third set. Also the first plague of the third set (hail) is announced 'early in the morning', not at the Nile.
evidence: Rashbam on Exodus 7:26: 'Moses warned Pharaoh twice before a plague materialised, whereas before the third plague he did not give any warning. This remained the pattern throughout all the plagues which occurred in groups of three' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashbam_on_Exodus.7.26); Exodus 7:15 'at the edge of the Nile'; 8:16 'as he is coming out to the water'; 9:13 'Early in the morning present yourself to Pharaoh' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.9.13)
fix: Then the plagues begin in earnest. Commentators such as Rashbam note that they come in sets of three: Pharaoh is warned before the first two plagues of each set, and the third comes without warning. This portion covers the first two sets and the first plague of the third.

current: Maimonides (in Hilchot Teshuva) argues that God's hardening of Pharaoh's heart after the first five plagues was itself a punishment: Pharaoh had used his free will to sin so grievously that he forfeited the ability to repent, a divine withdrawal of the capacity for return.
problem: Maimonides (Teshuvah 6:3) makes the punishment argument but says nothing about 'the first five plagues'; the five-plague point comes from the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 13:3) and Rashi on 7:3.
evidence: Mishneh Torah, Repentance 6:3: 'Since, he began to sin on his own initiative and caused hardships to the Israelites... judgment obligated that he be prevented from repenting' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Mishneh_Torah,_Repentance.6.3); Rashi on Exodus 7:3: 'in the case of the first five plagues it is not stated, "The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart"' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Exodus.7.3)
fix: Maimonides (Laws of Repentance 6:3) argues that God's hardening of Pharaoh's heart was itself a punishment: Pharaoh had first sinned by his own free will, so justice required that he be kept from repenting. Rashi (on 7:3) adds that for the first five plagues the Torah says only that Pharaoh's heart was hardened, not that God hardened it.

current: At the Passover seder, ten drops of wine are removed from the full cup — one for each plague — because our joy cannot be complete while others suffered, even enemies who oppressed us.
problem: The custom recorded by the Rema is sixteen drops (at 'blood, fire and smoke', at each of the ten plagues, and at Rabbi Yehuda's three-word mnemonic), not ten. The 'joy cannot be complete' reason is a popular modern explanation, not the one the codes give; the Darkhei Moshe links spilling with a finger to 'the finger of God' (Exodus 8:15).
evidence: Rema on Shulchan Arukh OC 473:7: 'ונוהגין לזרוק מעט מן הכוס באצבעו כשמגיע לדם ואש ותמרות עשן וכן כשמזכיר המכות דצ"ך עד"ש באח"ב... הכל י"ו פעמים' (spill a little from the cup with the finger... sixteen times) (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Shulchan_Arukh,_Orach_Chayim.473.7?version=hebrew); Darkhei Moshe OC 473 connects the finger to 'אצבע אלהים הוא' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Darkhei_Moshe,_Orach_Chayim.473?version=hebrew)
fix: At the Passover seder it is customary to spill a little wine from the cup as the plagues are named; the Rema (Orach Chayim 473:7) records sixteen drops in all, one for each plague and more for related words. A popular explanation is that our joy cannot be complete while others suffered.

current: The Israelites are commanded to mark their doorposts with lamb's blood so the angel of death will pass over them — the origin of Passover. Pharaoh finally releases the Israelites, who leave Egypt after 430 years.
problem: The verse says God passes over and does not let 'the Destroyer' enter; 'angel of death' is a later gloss (the Haggadah stresses God acted 'not by an angel'). '430 years' in Egypt is the plain wording of 12:40, but Rashi (and Seder Olam) count the 430 years from the Covenant Between the Parts, with far fewer years in Egypt itself; the app's own date bar follows that tradition.
evidence: Exodus 12:23 'GOD will pass over the door and not let the Destroyer enter and smite your home'; 12:40 'The length of time that the Israelites lived in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.12.23); Rashi on 12:40: 'Altogether from the birth of Isaac until now were 400 years... It is impossible to say that this means that they were 430 years in the land of Egypt alone' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Exodus.12.40)
fix: The Israelites are commanded to mark their doorposts with lamb's blood so that God will pass over their homes, the origin of Passover. Pharaoh finally releases the Israelites; the Torah dates this to the end of 430 years (12:40-41), which Rashi counts from God's covenant with Abraham rather than from the arrival in Egypt.

current: The Israelites leave on the fifteenth of Nissan having been in Egypt exactly 430 years.
problem: States one reading as fact; Rashi and Seder Olam reject 430 years in Egypt. The 15th of the month is from Numbers 33:3, not this parsha (fine), but the 430-year claim needs attribution.
evidence: Exodus 12:41 'at the end of the four hundred and thirtieth year, to the very day, all the ranks of GOD departed'; Rashi on 12:40 'It is impossible to say that this means that they were 430 years in the land of Egypt alone' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Exodus.12.40)
fix: The Israelites leave on the fifteenth of Nissan, 'at the end of the four hundred and thirtieth year' (12:41); Rashi explains that the 430 years are counted from God's covenant with Abraham, not from the arrival in Egypt.

current: Egyptian texts record the significance of firstborn sons as heirs and as ritual figures — the death of Pharaoh's firstborn would have been understood as the destruction of the royal succession itself, a blow to the theological claims of divine kingship that undergirded the entire Egyptian state. The timing of the Exodus at night, the urgency of departure, and the miraculous sea crossing have parallels in Egyptian records of Semitic groups being expelled or fleeing from Egypt in periods of political instability, though no Egyptian record names the biblical Exodus directly.
problem: No source found for Egyptian texts treating firstborn sons as 'ritual figures'; the royal-succession reading is speculation stated as fact. No Egyptian record describes a miraculous sea crossing, and the sea crossing is in Beshalach, not Bo.
evidence: No Egyptian source for a sea crossing or for firstborn sons as 'ritual figures' located. Wikipedia, Hyksos: kings of the Fifteenth Dynasty 'fl. c. 1650 – c. 1550 BC', seated at Avaris in the Nile Delta, of 'probable West Semitic, Levantine origin' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyksos); Wikipedia, Sources and parallels of the Exodus, discusses the Hyksos expulsion as a possible memory behind the story (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sources_and_parallels_of_the_Exodus)
fix: No Egyptian record names the biblical Exodus. Some scholars compare it with the end of the Hyksos, rulers of probable Semitic origin who governed the Nile Delta from Avaris until about 1550 BCE.

current: The Passover seder is the most widely practiced Jewish ritual in the world — a structured retelling of this night, with the Haggadah as its script.
problem: No worldwide measure supports 'the most widely practiced'. The largest survey (Pew 2020, US) finds the seder among the most common practices (62%) but below eating traditional Jewish foods (72%).
evidence: Pew Research Center, Jewish Americans in 2020: 62% held or attended a Seder in the past year; 72% cook or eat traditional Jewish foods (https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2021/05/11/jewish-americans-in-2020/)
fix: The Passover seder is one of the most widely observed Jewish rituals: a structured retelling of this night, with the Haggadah as its script.

current: the four cups of wine represent the four expressions of liberation in this portion.
problem: The four expressions of redemption are in Exodus 6:6-7, in Vaera, not in Bo.
evidence: Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 10:1: 'From where the Four Cups? Rebbi Joḥanan in the name of Rebbi Benaiah: Corresponding to the four deliveries: ...I shall take you out... I shall save you, I shall free you, I shall take you' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Jerusalem_Talmud_Pesachim.10.1); Exodus 6:6-7 'I will free you... deliver you... redeem you... take you to be My people' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.6.6-7)
fix: and the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim 10:1) links the four cups of wine to the four expressions of redemption in Exodus 6:6-7.

current: The Song of the Sea (Shirat HaYam) is written in the Torah scroll in a unique visual pattern — staggered 'brick' formation rather than regular columns — and is one of the few passages in the Torah where the layout itself is considered part of the sacred text.
problem: The Talmud says the brick layout applies to 'all of the songs in the Bible' (only two exceptions), so it is special, not unique.
evidence: Megillah 16b: 'All of the songs in the Bible are written in the form of a half brick arranged upon a whole brick and a whole brick arranged upon a half brick' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Megillah.16b)
fix: The Song of the Sea (Shirat HaYam) is written in the Torah scroll in a special staggered layout the Talmud (Megillah 16b) calls 'a half brick upon a whole brick', and it is one of the few passages in the Torah whose layout on the page is prescribed.

current: The Song of the Sea is recited every morning in the Jewish prayer service as part of the Shacharit liturgy — making this song the most frequently recited biblical poem in Jewish practice, heard over 365 times a year by observant Jews.
problem: Psalm 145 (Ashrei) is recited three times a day, so it, not the Song of the Sea, is the most frequently recited biblical poem.
evidence: Berakhot 4b: 'Anyone who recites: "A Psalm of David" (Psalms 145) three times every day is assured of a place in the World-to-Come' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Berakhot.4b)
fix: The Song of the Sea is recited every morning in the Shacharit prayer service, so observant Jews say it every day of the year.

current: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 91b) records that even unborn souls sang at the Sea — a poetic way of saying the miracle was so total that all of Israel, past and future, participated.
problem: Wrong page: Sanhedrin 91b uses 'then Moses will sing' as a proof of resurrection. The unborn teaching is Rabbi Meir's in Sotah 30b (and Berakhot 50a), and it is about fetuses in the womb, not 'souls... past and future'.
evidence: Sotah 30b: 'Rabbi Meir would say: From where is it derived that even fetuses in their mother's womb recited the song at the sea?' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sotah.30b); Sanhedrin 91b: 'Rabbi Meir said: From where is resurrection of the dead derived from the Torah?... "Then Moses... will sing"' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sanhedrin.91b)
fix: The Talmud (Sotah 30b) records Rabbi Meir's teaching that even babies still in their mothers' wombs sang the song at the Sea.

current: Moses bursts into song — the Song of the Sea, one of the oldest and most celebrated poems in Hebrew — and Miriam, his sister, leads the women in dance with timbrels.
problem: 'One of the oldest' is a scholarly dating judgment (based on archaic language) stated as fact; it should be attributed. Also 15:20 calls Miriam 'Aaron's sister' (tradition and Numbers 26:59 make her Moses's sister too, so 'his sister' is acceptable).
evidence: Exodus 15:20 'Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.15.20); Wikipedia, Song of the sea: 'Some scholars consider it the oldest surviving text describing the Exodus, dating to the pre-monarchic period' but others say 'it was deliberately written in an archaic style'; 'proposed dates for its composition range from the 13th to the 5th century BCE' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_the_sea)
fix: Moses bursts into song, the Song of the Sea, whose archaic Hebrew leads some scholars to consider it one of the oldest poems in the Bible, and Miriam, his sister, leads the women in dance with hand-drums.

current: Moses ascends and receives the Ten Commandments, which are proclaimed to all the people.
problem: In Yitro God speaks the Ten Commandments to the people from the mountain (20:1); Moses is told to come up to receive the stone tablets only later, in Mishpatim (24:12), and receives them in Ki Tisa (31:18).
evidence: Exodus 20:1 'God spoke all these words, saying'; Exodus 24:12 'Come up to Me on the mountain... and I will give you the stone tablets' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.20.1, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.24.12)
fix: God speaks the Ten Commandments from the mountain to all the people.

current: Jethro — a Midianite priest, an outsider — arrives with Moses's wife and sons and is overwhelmed hearing the story of the Exodus; he prostrates himself and acknowledges that YHWH is greater than all gods.
problem: It is Moses who bows to Jethro; Jethro rejoices and blesses God. Nothing says Jethro prostrated himself.
evidence: Exodus 18:7 'Moses went out to meet his father-in-law; he bowed low and kissed him'; 18:9-11 'And Jethro rejoiced... "Blessed be GOD"... "Now I know that GOD is greater than all gods"' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.18.7-11)
fix: Jethro, a Midianite priest and an outsider, arrives with Moses's wife and sons; Moses bows to him, tells him the story of the Exodus, and Jethro rejoices, blesses God and says, 'Now I know that YHWH is greater than all gods.'

current: The Ten Commandments appear twice in the Torah — here in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5 — with one significant difference: the Exodus version says to 'remember' (zachor) the Sabbath, while Deuteronomy says to 'guard' (shamor) it.
problem: There are several differences, not one: Deuteronomy grounds Shabbat in the Exodus from Egypt rather than creation, and changes the coveting commandment (wife listed first, 'crave', adds 'field').
evidence: Exodus 20:11 'For in six days GOD made heaven and earth... therefore GOD blessed the sabbath day'; Deuteronomy 5:15 'Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt... therefore... commanded you to observe the sabbath day'; 5:18 'you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not crave your neighbor's house, or field' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Deuteronomy.5.14-18)
fix: The Ten Commandments appear twice in the Torah, here in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5, with several differences; the best known is that Exodus says to 'remember' (zachor) the Sabbath, while Deuteronomy says to 'guard' (shamor) it.

current: The Friday night Shabbat hymn Lecha Dodi resolves this by declaring that both words were spoken simultaneously by God — something humanly impossible, representing the collapse of language before the divine.
problem: The simultaneous-utterance teaching comes from the Talmud, which Lecha Dodi quotes; 'representing the collapse of language' is the writer's own gloss. Smallest change: attribute to the Talmud and use its words.
evidence: Rosh Hashanah 27a: '"Remember the Shabbat day" (Exodus 20:8) and "Keep the Shabbat day" (Deuteronomy 5:12), were spoken by God simultaneously in a single utterance, something that the human mouth cannot speak and the human ear cannot hear' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rosh_Hashanah.27a)
fix: The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 27a) teaches that God spoke both words in a single utterance, 'something that the human mouth cannot speak and the human ear cannot hear', and the Friday night hymn Lecha Dodi repeats this: 'Shamor and zachor in a single utterance.'

current: The Ugaritic texts describe the storm-god Baal appearing in exactly these terms. Sinai itself has been proposed at multiple locations in the peninsula and beyond, with the traditional site at Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula attracting pilgrims for millennia; a monastery (St. Catherine's) has stood at this site since the 6th century CE.
problem: 'Exactly these terms' overstates it: the Baal texts share the thunder voice and quaking earth, not the full Sinai scene. The earliest documented pilgrim to Jebel Musa is Egeria, c. 381-384 CE, so 'for millennia' overstates about 1,600 years.
evidence: Baal Cycle KTU 1.4 VII: 'At his holy voice the earth quaked; at the issue of his lips the mountains were afraid' (Putrawan, Verbum et Ecclesia, https://verbumetecclesia.org.za/index.php/ve/article/view/3787/9803); Wikipedia, Saint Catherine's Monastery: Egeria's journal 'about 381/2–386'; monastery 'built between 548 and 565' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine%27s_Monastery)
fix: The Ugaritic texts describe the storm-god Baal in similar terms: 'At his holy voice the earth quaked.' Sinai itself has been proposed at many locations in the peninsula and beyond; the traditional site, Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, has drawn pilgrims since at least the 4th century CE, and St. Catherine's Monastery has stood at its foot since the 6th century CE.

current: Jethro's role is celebrated: his portion is the only parsha in the Torah named after a non-Israelite, and his advice on governance is cited as the model for Jewish communal leadership structures for millennia.
problem: Balak (Numbers 22:2), named after the Moabite king, and Noach are also named after non-Israelites. No source found for the 'model for millennia' claim.
evidence: Numbers 22:2 'Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites' (first words of parashat Balak) (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.22.2)
fix: Jethro's role is celebrated: this portion, which contains the Ten Commandments, is named after a Midianite priest, one of only a few parshiot (with Noach and Balak) named after someone outside Israel.

current: a Hebrew slave must go free after six years; if someone strikes another and they die, it is murder; if a thief cannot repay, he may be sold; an ox that gores must be stoned; if a man seduces a virgin, he must marry or pay a bride price.
problem: The Torah immediately distinguishes an unintended killing (the killer flees to a place of refuge), so 'it is murder' is wrong for that case. The ox is stoned only if it gores a person to death.
evidence: Exodus 21:12-13 'One who fatally strikes another shall be put to death. If it was not by design... I will assign you a place to which that person can flee'; 21:28 'When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.21.12-13, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.21.28)
fix: a Hebrew slave must go free after six years; a deliberate killer is put to death, while someone who kills by accident may flee to a place of refuge; if a thief cannot repay, he may be sold; an ox that gores a person to death must be stoned; if a man seduces a virgin, he must pay the bride price and marry her unless her father refuses.

current: do not take a widow's garment as collateral;
problem: The ban on taking a widow's garment in pledge is Deuteronomy 24:17. Mishpatim says not to mistreat a widow or orphan, and to return a neighbor's pledged garment by sunset.
evidence: Exodus 22:21 'You shall not ill-treat any widow or orphan'; 22:25 'If you take your neighbor's garment in pledge, you must return it before the sun sets' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.22.20-26)
fix: do not mistreat a widow or orphan; if you take a neighbor's cloak as a pledge, return it before sunset;

current: Then seventy elders ascend the mountain and see God, and eat and drink in God's presence — a vision so extraordinary the Torah says only that they 'saw God' without describing what they saw.
problem: The Torah does describe part of what they saw: a sapphire-like pavement under God's feet. Aaron, Nadab and Abihu also go up with the elders (24:9).
evidence: Exodus 24:10-11 'and they saw the God of Israel—under whose feet was the likeness of a pavement of sapphire, like the very sky for purity... they beheld God, and they ate and drank' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.24.10-11)
fix: Then Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders go up the mountain and see the God of Israel, with something like a pavement of sapphire under God's feet, 'like the very sky for purity', and they eat and drink.

current: The laws in this portion include what is arguably the world's earliest legislation against price gouging and economic exploitation of the powerless, framed not as policy but as divine command.
problem: Mishpatim has no price-gouging law, and 'world's earliest' is unsupported: Hammurabi's much older code already limited debt-slavery (law 117). What Mishpatim does contain is a ban on charging interest to the poor.
evidence: Exodus 22:24 'If you lend money to My people, to the poor among you, do not act toward them as a creditor; exact no interest from them' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.22.20-26); Code of Hammurabi 117 (c. 1754 BCE): debt-slaves 'shall work for three years... and in the fourth year they shall be set free' (https://avalon.law.yale.edu/ancient/hamcode.asp)
fix: The laws in this portion also forbid charging interest when lending to the poor (Exodus 22:24), framed not as policy but as divine command.

current: Significant differences exist — Hebrew law limits slavery's duration and prohibits selling a person for a debt that isn't their own — suggesting an independent tradition with shared literary conventions.
problem: Hammurabi also limits debt-slavery (to three years, law 117), and Exodus itself allows a father to sell his daughter (21:7), so neither is a real difference. The 'independent tradition' conclusion is one scholarly view stated as the answer.
evidence: Code of Hammurabi 117: 'sell himself, his wife, his son, and daughter... they shall work for three years... and in the fourth year they shall be set free'; law 8: 'if the thief has nothing with which to pay he shall be put to death' (https://avalon.law.yale.edu/ancient/hamcode.asp); Exodus 21:7 'When someone sells their daughter as a slave'; 22:2 '[The thief] must make restitution, and if lacking the means, shall be sold for the theft' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.22.2)
fix: There are also differences: under Hammurabi a thief who could not pay was put to death (law 8), while in Exodus he is sold to repay the theft (22:2). Scholars still debate how the two traditions are related.

current: The prohibition on oppressing the stranger appears thirty-six times in the Torah (more than any other commandment, according to some counts), always justified with the same reason: 'for you know the feelings of the stranger, having been strangers in Egypt.'
problem: The count is Rabbi Eliezer's in the Talmud (36, 'some say 46') and needs attribution; 'more than any other commandment' has no source there; and the reason is not always the same (the quoted wording is only in 23:9).
evidence: Bava Metzia 59b: 'Rabbi Eliezer the Great says: For what reason did the Torah issue warnings in thirty-six places, and some say in forty-six places, with regard to causing any distress to a convert?' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Bava_Metzia.59b); Exodus 23:9 'You shall not oppress a stranger, for you know the feelings of the stranger, having yourselves been strangers in the land of Egypt' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.23.9)
fix: The Talmud (Bava Metzia 59b) cites Rabbi Eliezer that the Torah warns against mistreating the stranger in thirty-six places (some say forty-six); here the reason is spelled out: 'for you know the feelings of the stranger, having yourselves been strangers in the land of Egypt' (23:9).

current: The 'blood of the covenant' ceremony — Moses sprinkling blood on the people — is one of only two blood-covenant rituals in the Torah, the other being circumcision.
problem: No source found for a count of 'two blood-covenant rituals'; the Torah does not call circumcision a blood covenant, and other rites involve blood (the Passover doorposts, the covenant between the pieces).
evidence: Exodus 24:8 'Moses took the blood and dashed it on the people and said, "This is the blood of the covenant that GOD now makes with you"' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.24.8); no source located for the 'only two' claim.
fix: In the 'blood of the covenant' ceremony, Moses dashes blood on the people and says, 'This is the blood of the covenant that YHWH now makes with you' (24:8).

current: After the dramatic legislation of Mishpatim and Moses's forty days on the mountain, God pivots to architecture:
problem: The Tabernacle instructions are spoken to Moses during his forty days on the mountain (24:18 then 25:1), not after them.
evidence: Exodus 24:18 'Moses remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights'; 25:1 'GOD spoke to Moses, saying' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.24.18)
fix: After the dramatic legislation of Mishpatim, with Moses now on the mountain for forty days, God pivots to architecture:

current: curtains of blue, purple, and crimson wool with embroidered cherubim,
problem: The verse says fine twisted linen together with blue, purple and crimson yarns, with cherubim worked in; Rashi says the cherubim were woven in, not embroidered.
evidence: Exodus 26:1 'fine twisted linen, of blue, purple, and crimson yarns, with a design of cherubim worked into them' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.26.1); Rashi on 26:1: 'Cherubim were figured on them in the process of weaving them, not afterwards by embroidery' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Exodus.26.1)
fix: curtains of fine linen and blue, purple, and crimson yarn with cherubim woven into them,

current: The Ark of the Covenant — aron ha-brit — is the most famous object in religious history and has inspired centuries of search and speculation about its location.
problem: 'The most famous object in religious history' is an unsourced superlative.
evidence: No source found for the superlative.
fix: The Ark of the Covenant (aron ha-brit) has inspired centuries of search and speculation about its location.

current: The menorah blueprint — beaten from a single piece of gold, with almond-blossom shaped cups — would represent between 75 and 100 pounds of pure gold.
problem: The one talent of gold covers the menorah together with its tongs and pans, not the menorah alone, and the pound figure depends on a modern estimate of the talent that is not cited.
evidence: Exodus 25:39 'It shall be made, with all these furnishings, out of a talent of pure gold' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.25.39)
fix: The menorah, beaten from a single piece of gold with almond-blossom shaped cups, was to be made together with its tongs and pans from one talent of pure gold (25:39).

current: Egyptian military campaigns included portable divine barques and shrines that traveled with the army, housing divine images for consultation and protection. The 'Tent of Meeting' concept has parallels in Ugaritic literature and across the ancient Near East.
problem: No source found for barque shrines housing images 'for consultation' on campaign. The parallel scholars actually draw (Michael Homan) is to Ramesses II's royal war tent and camp at Kadesh, shown in Egyptian temple reliefs.
evidence: Homan, 'The Divine Warrior in His Tent' (BAR): the closest model is 'the tent and military camp of Pharaoh Ramesses II during the battle of Kadesh... about 1275 BCE'; both have courtyards 'twice as long as they are wide' with the entrance in the east and a 2:1 reception tent leading to a square throne tent (https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/article/the-divine-warrior-in-his-tent/, summary via https://www.thetorah.com/article/the-tabernacle-in-its-ancient-near-eastern-context)
fix: Portable royal tents were known in the ancient world: Egyptian temple reliefs show the camp of Ramesses II at the battle of Kadesh (c. 1275 BCE), with a courtyard twice as long as it is wide, an entrance on the east, and an inner square throne room, a layout scholars such as Michael Homan compare to the Tabernacle.

current: Purple dye (tekhelet) was extracted from murex sea snails and was extraordinarily expensive.
problem: Tekhelet is the blue (blue-violet) dye; the purple is argaman. Both came from murex-type sea snails.
evidence: Wikipedia, Tekhelet: 'Modern scholars believe that tekhelet probably referred to blue to blue-purple colors'; argaman is 'a Biblical reddish-purple dye'; both from Mediterranean sea snails (Hexaplex trunculus; Bolinus brandaris) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekhelet)
fix: The blue (tekhelet) and purple (argaman) dyes were made from murex sea snails and were extraordinarily expensive.

current: The three portions describing the Tabernacle's design (Terumah, Tetzaveh, and part of Ki Tisa) have generated more medieval commentary than almost any other section of Torah — partly because they seem repetitive and partly because their spiritual significance is not obvious.
problem: No source found for the comparative claim about volume of medieval commentary.
evidence: No source found.
fix: Cut the sentence.

current: The Midrash reads every detail symbolically: the three layers of the Ark represent Torah wrapped in scholarship wrapped in fear of God.
problem: No midrash found with this reading. The Talmud does discuss the Ark's three layers (Yoma 72b) and draws a different lesson from the gold inside and out.
evidence: Yoma 72b: 'Bezalel made three arks: A middle one made of wood... an inner one made of gold... and an outer one of gold'; 'Rava said: This alludes to the idea that any Torah scholar whose inside is not like his outside... is not to be considered a Torah scholar' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Yoma.72b)
fix: The rabbis read the details symbolically: the Talmud (Yoma 72b) says the Ark was three nested boxes, gold, wood and gold, and learns from the gold inside and out that a Torah scholar's inside must match his outside.

current: The voluntary nature of the donation — from those whose hearts moved them — became the model for all Jewish charitable giving: tzedakah must come from genuine generosity.
problem: In Jewish law tzedakah is an obligation that a community may even enforce on the wealthy, so it is not purely voluntary.
evidence: Bava Batra 8b: 'they can collect charity by force'; 'Rava compelled Rav Natan bar Ami and took four hundred dinars from him for charity' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Bava_Batra.8b)
fix: The Tabernacle gifts were voluntary, taken only from 'every person whose heart moves them' (25:2).

current: Moses himself is conspicuously absent from this portion — his name does not appear anywhere in it, the only such Torah portion after his introduction — while Aaron and his sons take center stage as the priestly dynasty is established.
problem: Several Deuteronomy portions (Eikev, Shoftim, Ki Teitzei, Nitzavim) also never use the name Moses; the traditional claim, as the Baal HaTurim puts it, excludes Deuteronomy.
evidence: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Exodus 27:20: 'לא הזכיר משה בזה הסדר משא"כ בכל החומש שמשעה שנולד משה אין סדר שלא הוזכר בה (חוץ ממשנה תורה)' (Moses is not mentioned in this portion, unlike the whole Torah where from Moses's birth no portion lacks him, except Deuteronomy) (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Kitzur_Baal_HaTurim_on_Exodus.27.20?version=hebrew); count of the word משה in Sefaria's Hebrew text: Tetzaveh 0, Eikev 0, Shoftim 0, Ki Teitzei 0, Nitzavim 0 (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Deuteronomy.7.12-11.25?version=hebrew etc.)
fix: Moses himself is conspicuously absent from this portion: his name does not appear anywhere in it, the only portion from his birth to the end of Numbers without it, while Aaron and his sons take center stage as the priestly dynasty is established.

current: sprinkles blood on their garments — and the priests must remain at the Tabernacle entrance for all seven days without leaving.
problem: The instruction to stay at the Tent's entrance for seven days is given in Leviticus 8:33; Tetzaveh says only that the ordination takes seven days (29:35).
evidence: Exodus 29:35 'You shall ordain them through seven days'; Leviticus 8:33 'You shall not go outside the entrance of the Tent of Meeting for seven days' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.29.35, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.8.33)
fix: sprinkles blood on their garments, and the ordination is repeated for seven days.

current: The golden incense altar that closes the portion is the only altar at which blood is never poured: its function is purely olfactory, turning sweet incense smoke toward heaven daily.
problem: The same passage requires Aaron to put blood of the purgation offering on the incense altar's horns once a year, so it is not 'purely' for incense.
evidence: Exodus 30:10 'Once a year Aaron shall perform purification upon its horns with blood of the purgation offering' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.30.10)
fix: The golden incense altar that closes the portion is for incense, burned every morning and evening, not for animal offerings; only once a year is blood put on its horns (30:10).

current: This is the only parsha in the entire Torah after Shemot (Exodus 1) in which Moses's name does not appear — a fact the rabbis connected to Moses's plea 'erase me from your book' in the next portion (Ki Tisa), arguing that a righteous person's words are never entirely in vain.
problem: Several Deuteronomy portions also lack the name (see finding on narrativeSummary). The Baal HaTurim's reason is that 'a sage's curse, even a conditional one, comes true', not that a righteous person's words are 'never in vain'.
evidence: Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Exodus 27:20: 'והטעם משום שאמר מחני נא מספרך אשר כתבת וקללת חכם אפי' על תנאי באה ונתקיים בזה' (the reason: he said 'erase me from Your book', and a sage's curse, even conditional, comes true) (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Kitzur_Baal_HaTurim_on_Exodus.27.20?version=hebrew)
fix: From Moses's birth to the end of Numbers, this is the only parsha in which his name does not appear. The Baal HaTurim connects this to Moses's plea 'erase me from Your book' in the next portion (Ki Tisa), citing the rule that a sage's curse comes true even when it was conditional.

current: The concept of a breastplate bearing the names or symbols of constituent groups — worn over the heart during divine consultation — has parallels in Egyptian priestly practice.
problem: No source found for an Egyptian breastplate bearing names of groups used in divine consultation.
evidence: No source found.
fix: Cut the sentence.

current: the robe atoned for improper speech (its bells would ring to announce the priest and thereby prevent surprise violations), the breastplate atoned for errors in judgment, the turban for arrogance, the tunic for bloodshed.
problem: The Talmud's reason is that a garment that makes sound (bells) atones for a sin of sound (evil speech), not that the bells prevented 'surprise violations'. 'Errors in judgment' should be 'improper judgments' (the breastplate of judgment).
evidence: Arakhin 16a: 'The breastplate of the High Priest atones for improper judgments... The robe of the High Priest atones for malicious speech, as the Holy One, Blessed be He says: Let an item that produces sound, i.e., the bells of the robe, come and atone for an act of malicious sound'; 'the tunic atones for bloodshed' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Arakhin.16a)
fix: the robe, with its ringing bells, atoned for malicious speech, a sound atoning for a sound; the breastplate of judgment atoned for improper judgments; the turban for arrogance; the tunic for bloodshed (Arakhin 16a).

current: He destroys the calf and thousands die in a plague.
problem: About three thousand are killed by the Levites (32:28); the plague (32:35) is given no death toll.
evidence: Exodus 32:28 'The men of Levi did as Moses had bidden; and some three thousand of the people fell that day'; 32:35 'Then GOD sent a plague upon the people' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.32.28, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.32.35)
fix: He destroys the calf; the Levites kill about three thousand people, and God strikes the people with a plague.

current: Moses has been gone forty days and the people below crack:
problem: The Torah says only that Moses was 'so long in coming down'; Rashi explains the people miscounted and thought the forty days were over when they were not.
evidence: Exodus 32:1 'When the people saw that Moses was so long in coming down from the mountain' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.32.1); Rashi on 32:1: 'They thought that the day on which he ascended the mountain... was to be included in this number' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Exodus.32.1)
fix: Moses is late coming down from the mountain, and the people below crack:

current: the rabbis justified it through analogy: if a king's engagement contract arrives and the bride is found to be unfaithful, it is better to tear it up before she sees the terms of what she has violated.
problem: In the Midrash the agent tears the marriage contract so that the bride 'be judged as a single woman and not as a married woman', i.e. to lessen her guilt, not to keep her from seeing the terms.
evidence: Shemot Rabbah 43:1: 'a prince who sent to betroth a woman through an intermediary. She went and strayed with another man. The intermediary... ripped it. He said: It is preferable that she be judged as a single woman and not as a married woman. So did Moses' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Shemot_Rabbah.43.1)
fix: the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 43:1) justifies it with a parable: when a prince's bride was unfaithful before the wedding, his agent tore up the marriage contract, saying it was better that she be judged as a single woman than as a married one.

current: Excavations at Dan and Bethel in northern Israel unearthed golden calves associated with Jeroboam's shrines (10th century BCE), set up with almost the same words used here: 'These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt' — suggesting the biblical editor is explicitly connecting those later shrines to the golden calf sin.
problem: No golden calves have been found at Dan or Bethel. The calves are known from 1 Kings 12; at Tel Dan excavators found a cult compound with a large horned altar. The editorial link is a scholarly reading and should be hedged.
evidence: 1 Kings 12:28 'the king... made two golden calves. He said to the people... "This is your god, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt!"' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/I_Kings.12.28); Wikipedia, Tel Dan: 'Excavations at the cultic area of Dan have revealed a religious compound with a large four-horned central altar' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Dan)
fix: The book of Kings says that in the 10th century BCE Jeroboam set up golden calves at Dan and Bethel with almost the same words used here, 'This is your god, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt' (1 Kings 12:28), and many scholars think the golden calf story was told with those shrines in mind. At Tel Dan, archaeologists have uncovered a sacred compound with a large horned altar, but no calf.

current: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 102a) says there is no punishment that befalls Israel that does not contain some measure of the golden calf, meaning it is the 'original sin' of the Jewish people.
problem: The Talmud's statement is accurate (a 'one twenty-fourth' share), but 'original sin' is a Christian theological term the source does not use and that implies more than it says.
evidence: Sanhedrin 102a: 'Rabbi Yitzḥak says: You have no punishment that comes to the world in which there is not one twenty-fourth of the surplus of a litra of the first calf' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sanhedrin.102a)
fix: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 102a) says that every punishment that comes to the world contains a small share of the punishment for the golden calf.

current: so much that the craftsmen have to tell Moses the people must be restrained from bringing more.
problem: The craftsmen report that the people are bringing more than needed; it is Moses who orders the proclamation to stop.
evidence: Exodus 36:5-6 'and said to Moses, "The people are bringing more than is needed..." Moses thereupon had this proclamation made throughout the camp: "Not a single man or woman should make further effort toward gifts for the sanctuary!"' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.36.5-6)
fix: so much that the craftsmen tell Moses the people are bringing more than is needed, and Moses has it announced through the camp that they should stop.

current: Bezalel's name means literally 'in the shadow of God' — be-tzel-El — and the Talmud (Berachot 55a) credits him with knowing the kabbalistic combination of Hebrew letters by which God created heaven and earth, which is why he could build something capable of housing the divine presence.
problem: The Talmud says Bezalel 'knew how to join the letters with which heaven and earth were created'; calling it 'kabbalistic' is anachronistic and the 'which is why he could build...' conclusion is not in the source (it derives the point from the shared words wisdom, understanding and knowledge).
evidence: Berakhot 55a: 'Rav Yehuda said that Rav said: Bezalel knew how to join the letters with which heaven and earth were created' and 'Perhaps you were in God's shadow [betzel El]' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Berakhot.55a)
fix: Bezalel's name can be read 'in the shadow of God' (be-tzel El), a pun the Talmud itself makes (Berakhot 55a), and the same page says Bezalel 'knew how to join the letters with which heaven and earth were created.'

current: Temple construction in the ancient Near East was uniformly understood as a communal, divinely directed project: Sumerian, Akkadian, and Egyptian texts describe divine blueprints revealed in dreams and broad public participation in sacred building.
problem: 'Uniformly' and the Egyptian/Akkadian claims are unsourced; the classic example is the Sumerian Gudea Cylinders.
evidence: Wikipedia, Gudea cylinders: 'dating to c. 2125 BC'; in Gudea's dream a figure holding 'a lapis lazuli tablet' showed 'the plan of a house'; afterwards 'Gudea then instructs the people of Lagash' and lays the first brick (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudea_cylinders)
fix: Other ancient Near Eastern texts also describe temples built to a divine plan: in the Sumerian Gudea Cylinders (c. 2125 BCE), King Gudea of Lagash is shown the plan of the god Ningirsu's temple in a dream and then calls the people of his city to build it.

current: a display of financial transparency remarkable for antiquity and suggesting Moses was protecting himself against accusations of misappropriation.
problem: The motive is not stated in the Torah; it is the Midrash's reading and should be attributed.
evidence: Shemot Rabbah 51:6: 'When the labor of the Sanctuary was completed, he said to them: Come and I will make an accounting before you... Now Israel will find justification to say that...' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Shemot_Rabbah.51.6)
fix: The Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 51:6) says Moses gave this public accounting so that no one could suspect him of taking any of the donations.

current: The repeated phrase 'as YHWH commanded Moses' appears eighteen times in the construction narrative — corresponding, according to the Midrash, to the eighteen vertebrae of the spine, the column that enables a human being to stand upright before God.
problem: The eighteen count is right, but the Jerusalem Talmud links it to the eighteen blessings of the Amidah, not to the vertebrae; the vertebrae are a separate reason for the eighteen blessings (Berakhot 28b), and 'stand upright before God' is added.
evidence: Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 4:3 (reasons for eighteen benedictions): 'Rebbi Samuel bar Naḥmani in the name of Rebbi Yoḥanan: Corresponding to the eighteen times "commandment" is mentioned in the second description of the tabernacle' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.4.3); Sefaria Hebrew of Exodus 38:21-40:38 has 17 'צוה יהוה את משה' plus 40:16 'צוה יהוה אתו' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.38.21-40.38?version=hebrew)
fix: The phrase 'as YHWH commanded Moses' appears eighteen times in this account of the construction, and the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot 4:3) connects these eighteen mentions to the eighteen blessings of the Amidah prayer.

current: the Midrash (Tanchuma Pekudei 11) states that when the Mishkan was erected, it was as if the world was created anew. Each element's creation — light (menorah), water (laver), bread (showbread table), incense (altar) — recapitulates the elements of creation.
problem: The teaching is in Tanchuma Pekudei 2, not 11, and it says the Tabernacle is 'equal to the creation of the world', pairing it with the days of creation: curtains with the heavens, the veil with the firmament, the laver with the gathered waters, the menorah with the lights, the cherubim with the birds, the high priest with man. Bread and incense are not in its list.
evidence: Midrash Tanchuma, Pekudei 2: 'the Tabernacle is equal to the creation of the world itself... curtains... the veil shall divide... a laver of brass... put water therein... a candlestick of pure gold... the cherubim shall spread out their wings... A man who is a high priest' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Midrash_Tanchuma,_Pekudei.2)
fix: The Midrash (Tanchuma Pekudei 2) says the Tabernacle is equal to the creation of the world, and pairs its parts with the days of creation: the curtains with the heavens, the veil with the firmament that divides, the laver's water with the gathered seas, the menorah with the sun and moon, the cherubim's wings with the birds, and the high priest with the first human.

current: The priestly blessing with which Moses blesses the completed Tabernacle workers (Numbers 6, quoted here) is still pronounced in synagogues by kohanim today.
problem: Exodus 39:43 says only that Moses blessed them; Numbers 6 is not quoted. Rashi gives the blessing's words, and it is not the priestly blessing.
evidence: Exodus 39:43 'And when Moses saw that they had performed all the tasks... Moses blessed them' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.39.43); Rashi on 39:43: 'He said to them "May it be the will of God that His Shechinah rest upon the work of your hands"' (https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Exodus.39.43)
fix: When the work is done, Moses blesses the people (39:43); Rashi says the blessing was 'May it be the will of God that His Presence rest upon the work of your hands.'
